subject: mathematics
question_text: If a, b, c are the position vectors of the vertices A, B, C respectively of triangle ABC, find the vector equation of the median through the vertex A.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.61, chapter 6 ADDITION OF VECTORS, Very Short Answer question 14. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 shape is the one this bank uses for a Maths-1A Section A question: the first mark is for identifying the second point of the median as the midpoint of BC, the second for writing the two-point form of the line. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — Addition of Vectors has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1 to Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The answer was checked at both ends: t = 0 returns a, the vertex A, and t = 1 returns (b + c)/2, the midpoint of BC, so the equation does describe the median. Taking t = 2/3 returns (a + b + c)/3, the centroid, which is the further check that the line is the correct one.

recall_prompt: Say how you would write the vector equation of a median — say which two points it joins.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find the midpoint of BC
steps.margin_note: First mark. 'Median through A' names only one point, so the second one has to be found: the midpoint D of BC, the side opposite A. Its position vector is the average of b and c.
steps.memory_tip: A median runs from a vertex to the midpoint of the OPPOSITE side. The midpoint of BC is the average (b + c)/2.
lines: The median through A joins A to the
midpoint D of the opposite side BC.

recall.must_convey: That the median through A ends at the midpoint D of BC, whose position vector is (b + c)/2.
accept: the median goes from A to the midpoint of BC which is b plus c over two
find the midpoint of the opposite side first
D is the midpoint of BC so its position vector is the average of b and c
BC midpoint teeskovali, adi b plus c by two
the second point is the midpoint of the side opposite A

steps.why: A line needs two points and the question names only one. Finding the midpoint supplies the second, and that is the only place the word median is used.
common_mistakes: Taking the midpoint of AB or of AC instead of BC.
Writing the midpoint as b + c without dividing by 2.
Using the centroid (a + b + c)/3 as the second point.

steps.label: Write the two-point form
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two points and no direction given, so the two-point form is the one to use. t = 0 lands on A and t = 1 lands on D.
steps.memory_tip: Two points, so r = (1 − t)(first point) + t(second point). t = 0 sits at A, t = 1 sits at the midpoint.
lines: A has position vector a, and D has (b + c)/2,
so by the two-point form of a line,

recall.must_convey: That the equation is r = (1 − t)a + t(b + c)/2 with t real.
accept: r equals one minus t times a plus t times b plus c over two
use the two point form with A and the midpoint
r is one minus t into a plus t into the midpoint of BC
r equals one minus t a plus t times b plus c by two, t real
the two point form of the line through A and the midpoint

steps.why: The two-point form works because (1 − t) and t add to 1 for every value of t, and that sum being 1 is the test for a point lying on the line through A and D.
common_mistakes: Using r = a + tb as though b were a direction vector.
Dropping t ∈ R, which describes only the segment AD.
Writing r = (1 − t)a + (b + c)/2 with the t left off the second term.
